title: The tenth traveler
hookLine: ten cross a river and every count comes out nine
carry: the self is never lost, only overlooked
tomorrow: two glows, two doors, one jewel. who walks out rich?

cards: Group photos have an old problem: whoever holds the camera is never in the shot. The Panchadashi tells a much older version, and it's a puzzle. Ten travelers wade across a river.
On the far bank, one counts heads. Nine. Another counts.
Nine. Every count comes out nine, though nobody drowned. So they sit on the bank and weep for a friend who isn't lost.

teach.b: Each counter counted everyone except himself.
A passerby watches one more count and says one short sentence: you are the tenth. The story sits in the chapter called the lamp of contentment, Triptidipa, and the book walks through it slowly.
First the travelers simply don't see the tenth. Then they're sure there's no tenth. Then they grieve, and the grief is real, though nobody's gone.
Next comes the stranger's word: the tenth is here. They can believe it before they see it. Then the stranger has the counter count again, and when he reaches himself, he sees it directly.
I'm the tenth. The tears stop, and what's left is a plain gladness. That's the puzzle solved.
Nothing new was found. Only the knowing changed. The self, atman, was never lost, only overlooked.

In Advaita, that's how the self is known: not as something brought in from outside, but as the counter who was always counting. And notice the gap between hearing and seeing. A teacher's word can say the tenth is here.
The book says seeing it for yourself is what ends the grief. The stranger speaks a few words. The counter does the counting.

how: Advaita teachers tell the tenth-man story aloud to students, and the line 'you are the tenth' is used as a short way of pointing to the self.

s: in the story, one traveler really drowned and is found later
nobody drowned. each counter left out himself.
the Panchadashi says hearing 'you are the tenth' helps even before seeing it
they can believe it from the word; seeing it directly ends the grief.
in this story the self is found as something new, from outside
nothing new is found. only the knowing changes.

games.q: a friend is taking a gap year to 'go find herself' and asks what Advaita would say. what fits the tenth traveler?
o: the self isn't somewhere out there to find; it's the one doing the looking. enjoy the trip anyway.
keep searching; the self is out there somewhere, waiting to be found.
there's no self at all, so there's nothing to look for.
games.why: the tenth was never missing. nothing new was found; only the knowing changed.

practice: Count, slowly, a few people or things you're grateful for today, one for each breath. When the count feels finished, add one more: the one who's been doing the counting. Stay with that last one for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The Panchadashi: here, the book of the tenth traveler, who wept for the one doing the counting.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the tenth; the story is known as the tenth man.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the self is never lost, only overlooked. The missing tenth was the one counting all along.
